title: Foraging wild garlic in UK woodland and hedgerows
subtitle: Harvest, identification, and poisonous look-alikes
excerpt: Wild garlic carpets damp deciduous woodland across the UK from March to May. Leaves, flowers, and seed pods are all edible. This guide covers identification against two poisonous look-alikes and safe harvesting practice.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); John Wright, The Forager's Calendar (2019); BSBI species accounts for Allium ursinum; Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981; Theft Act 1968.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.
The specific habitat type where a wild plant grows, used as one of the three identification features.

content.text: Wild garlic (Allium ursinum) carpets the floor of damp deciduous woodland and sheltered hedgerow banks from March to May, filling the air with a sharp garlic scent. Leaves, flowers, and seed pods are all edible; leaves are the main harvest. Verify your identification before eating; if in doubt, do not eat.
Apply the
rule-of-three identification
method: confirm (1) the garlic scent when a leaf is crushed, (2) the smooth elliptical leaf with a single central vein, and (3) the woodland or hedgerow bank
foraging zone
. All three must match before you pick anything.
ID features
Scent: crush a leaf. A strong, clean garlic smell is the most reliable single feature. Lily of the valley has no garlic scent; autumn crocus has no scent.
Leaf: elliptical, smooth, bright green, 15 to 25 cm long, with a prominent central vein. Stalk is triangular in cross-section.
Habitat: damp, shaded deciduous woodland and hedgerow banks. Often carpets whole areas. Not in open grassland.
Flowers (May): white, six-petalled, in a round cluster on a single stem. Star-shaped at close range.
Poisonous look-alikes
Two
look-alike plants
grow in the same habitat and season. Both are toxic.
Lily of the valley (Convallaria majalis): similar elliptical leaf, same woodland habitat. No garlic scent. More parallel veins rather than a single central vein. Highly toxic.
Autumn crocus (Colchicum autumnale): leaves emerge without flowers in spring and look similar. No garlic scent. Leaf is narrower and more upright. Extremely toxic.
When and how to harvest

Pick from March to late April, before the plant flowers. Once it flowers, leaves become tougher and more bitter. Take the top one to three leaves per stem with scissors or secateurs; do not pull the plant out. Leave the bulb and most of the plant to regrow.
Flowers (May) are edible and work as a garnish. Seed pods (June) have a milder flavour and can be pickled. Take roughly a third of what you see and leave the rest for the plant to set seed.
After harvesting

Rinse in cold water. Leaves wilt quickly; use within 24 hours or blitz into pesto with oil for the fridge, where it keeps two to three days, or freeze it. Wild garlic is safe to eat raw; the scent and flavour soften with brief cooking.
Legal and ethical

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of foliage and flowers from hedgerows and common land for personal use. Uprooting the plant is an offence. Private land requires the landowner's permission. Sites of Special Scientific Interest carry stricter rules; check before foraging in designated areas.

rows.symptom: Not sure it smells like garlic
rows.cause: Leaf not crushed firmly enough, or the plant may be a look-alike
rows.fix: Crush a section of leaf between finger and thumb and smell immediately. A clear, strong garlic scent is the definitive test. If you cannot detect it, do not harvest.

rows.symptom: Leaves look right but habitat is open grassland
rows.cause: Wild garlic grows in woodland and hedgerow banks, not open grassland
rows.fix: Do not harvest. Confirm you are in damp, shaded deciduous woodland or a sheltered hedgerow bank before picking.

rows.cause: Possible misidentification, or eating too large a quantity on first try
rows.fix: Seek medical advice if symptoms go beyond mild discomfort. For future harvests, confirm all three rule-of-three features before picking and start with a small amount.
